content: Lung disease in preterm infants is frequently associated with lung edema, which complicates their condition. The primary goal of this review was to evaluate the risks and benefits of administering aerosolized diuretics to preterm infants who either have or are developing chronic lung disease (CLD). Specifically, the review aimed to assess the effects of this treatment on short-term outcomes, such as the need for oxygen or ventilatory support, as well as long-term outcomes. Secondary objectives included evaluating changes in pulmonary mechanics and identifying potential complications associated with the therapy. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE were searched for studies published between 1966 and 1998. Additional searches were conducted in July 2009 to update the findings. Abstract books from national and international societies in the United States and Europe were also hand-searched. The review included randomized trials involving preterm infants who were at least five days old and had either developed or were at risk of developing CLD. These infants were randomly assigned to receive aerosolized loop diuretics. The data collection and analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Collaboration. Both parallel and cross-over trials were included, and baseline and final outcome data measured on a continuous scale were transformed into change scores using Follmann's formula whenever possible. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. Most of these studies focused on pathophysiological parameters rather than clinically significant outcomes or potential complications of diuretic therapy. None of the studies evaluated the actual amount of diuretic delivered to the patient. Furosemide was the only diuretic used in all eight studies. For preterm infants younger than three weeks who were developing CLD, there was insufficient information to determine the effects of aerosolized furosemide on clinical outcomes or lung function. In preterm infants older than three weeks with established CLD, a single aerosolized dose of 1 mg/kg of furosemide appeared to transiently improve pulmonary mechanics. However, there was not enough evidence to evaluate the effects of chronic administration of aerosolized furosemide on oxygenation or pulmonary mechanics. The authors concluded that in preterm infants older than three weeks with CLD, a single dose of aerosolized furosemide can improve pulmonary mechanics. However, due to the lack of data from randomized trials assessing clinically significant outcomes, the routine or prolonged use of aerosolized loop diuretics in preterm infants with or at risk of developing CLD cannot be recommended based on the current evidence. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the clinically important effects of aerosolized diuretics.
